body:
Fixes #5986.

The docs for `insert()` promised the strong exception guarantee for every overload, but a failed copy of a new element could leave the value changed. With `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS`, the value was even left invalid: stale parent pointers made the next `assert_invariant()` abort. After the [discussion](https://github.com/nlohmann/json/pull/5996#issuecomment-6571792055) of what the standard containers guarantee, this PR no longer builds a rollback on top of `array_t`/`object_t`. Instead it documents the guarantees that `insert()` actually gives, and fixes the two places where it fell short of them.

### Changes (`basic_json::insert`)

- **`insert(pos, const basic_json&)`:** at `end()`, forwards as before (`std::vector` has no effects there). Anywhere else, copies the value first and inserts it by move, as libstdc++ does internally. libc++ shifts the tail before copying, so a failed copy left an extra `null` behind.
- **Parents:** `insert_iterator()` and the object `insert(first, last)` set the parents in a scope guard, which also runs when an exception is thrown. A failed insertion now leaves a valid value with `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS` as well. Without `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS` the guard does nothing.
- **Docs (`insert.md`):** strong guarantee for (1); basic guarantee for (2)–(5): if copying the new elements throws, the value may be partially modified but stays a valid array or object. The argument checks throw before anything changes. This matches what `std::vector::insert` ([vector.modifiers]) and `std::map::insert` ([associative.reqmts.except]) promise when copying `T` allocates, and what `update()` already documents.

### Tests

`unit-allocator.cpp`, "insert() provides its documented exception guarantees (#5986)": fails every allocation in turn for all overloads, with `json` and `ordered_json`, with and without spare capacity, inserting in the middle and at the end. For (1) it checks that `dump()` is unchanged. For (2)–(5) it checks that the value keeps its type, that every child names its parent, and that a copy succeeds.

Mutation checks: dropping the copy-first step fails the strong check on libc++, and dropping the guard aborts in `assert_invariant()` with `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS`. With the fix, the test passes on Apple clang (ASan+UBSan) and on GCC 16 (libstdc++, `-Wall -Wextra`, no warnings), with and without `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS`. The full `ctest` with ASan+UBSan passes 182/182. A program that calls every overload compiles and runs with `-fno-exceptions -DJSON_NOEXCEPTION`.

### Performance

Mac instruction counts from the A/B harness, develop → this PR. Each repetition copies a 100-element array or a 16-member object, then makes one insert (8-element sources):

| row | json | ordered_json |
|---|---|---|
| single int, middle / end | 1.007 / 1.005 | 1.007 / 1.006 |
| single string, middle / end | 1.008 / 1.005 | 1.006 / 1.005 |
| single array, middle | 0.998 | 1.006 |
| count int, middle / end | 1.000 / 0.991 | 1.000 / 1.000 |
| count string, middle | 1.000 | 0.995 |
| range int, middle / end | 1.000 / 1.000 | 1.000 / 1.000 |
| range string, middle / end | 0.995 / 0.995 | 1.000 / 1.000 |
| object range, 16 new / 3 new / 16 existing keys | 0.998 / 0.996 / 1.005 | 1.000 / 1.000 / 0.990 |

Every row is within 1 %. The single-element inserts pay about 40–60 instructions for the end check and the extra move. On the same workload, the previous version of this PR (rotate and rollback) cost +6–12 % on count and range inserts in the middle, and +2–5 % on object inserts into non-empty objects.

### Public API

No source or ABI changes. The documented exception guarantee of `insert()` overloads (2)–(5) is now basic instead of strong. This only documents what every 3.x release has done: the strong wording for these overloads arrived with the API docs in 3.10.0 and the code never provided it. Overload (1) now actually provides its strong guarantee.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

comments.body:
I don't like this solution as it is so verbose. Easier solutions have worse performance. Another idea would be to drop the strong exception guarantee which would not be a breaking change as it was apparently never properly working.

I'm looking forward to hearing your opinions.

I compared the strong guarantee that `insert()` documents with what the standard containers underneath promise. Short answer: for most overloads, we promise more than `std::vector` and `std::map` give us, and on develop `insert()` just forwards to them.

### What the standard promises

**`std::vector::insert`**, [[vector.modifiers]](https://eel.is/c++draft/vector.modifiers) (C++11: [23.3.6.5/1](https://timsong-cpp.github.io/cppwp/n3337/vector.modifiers#1)):

> If an exception is thrown other than by the copy constructor, move constructor, assignment operator, or move assignment operator of `T` or by any `InputIterator` operation, there are no effects. If an exception is thrown while inserting a single element at the end and `T` is *Cpp17CopyInsertable* or `is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>` is `true`, there are no effects.

So the vector rolls back only when the allocator fails, or for a single element inserted at the end. (C++11 has only the first sentence.) If `T`'s copy throws during an insert in the middle, a count insert or a range insert, all you get is the basic guarantee.

**`std::map` / `std::unordered_map`**, [[associative.reqmts.except]](https://eel.is/c++draft/associative.reqmts.except) and [[unord.req.except]](https://eel.is/c++draft/unord.req.except) (C++11: [23.2.4.1/2](https://timsong-cpp.github.io/cppwp/n3337/associative.reqmts.except#2)):

> if an exception is thrown by any operation from within an `insert` or `emplace` function inserting a single element, the insertion has no effect.

That covers single-element insertion only. Range `insert(first, last)` has no such guarantee.

### What this means for `basic_json`

The copy constructor of `basic_json` allocates, so a `bad_alloc` while copying elements counts as "thrown by the copy constructor of `T`". That is the case where `std::vector` doesn't roll back. Overload by overload:

| `insert` overload | what the standard guarantees | what we document |
|---|---|---|
| `insert(pos, const basic_json&)` at `end()` | strong | strong |
| `insert(pos, const basic_json&)` elsewhere | basic | strong |
| `insert(pos, basic_json&&)` | strong in effect: our move constructor is `noexcept`, so only the allocator can throw | strong |
| `insert(pos, cnt, val)` | basic | strong |
| `insert(pos, first, last)` | basic | strong |
| `insert(pos, ilist)` | basic: develop copies into a temporary `array_t` and then does a range insert from move iterators, which allocates only if it reallocates | strong |
| object `insert(first, last)` | basic: `std::map` range insert; `ordered_map::insert(first, last)` inserts one element at a time without rollback | strong |

The two standard libraries differ on the single-element case. libstdc++ copies `__x` into a `_Temporary_value` before shifting anything. libc++ (`__vector/vector.h`, `insert(const_iterator, const_reference)`) moves the tail first and then does `*__p = *__xr`. Our `operator=` takes its argument by value, so the copy throws after the shift, and the array ends up with an extra `null`. That's part of what the new test catches on libc++.

### Where the docs stand

The strong guarantee isn't old. The Doxygen comments in 3.5.0 said nothing about exception safety for `insert()`. The wording "Strong exception safety: if an exception occurs, the original value stays intact." arrived with the API docs page in fe89049aee (first released in 3.10.0) and was never backed by the code. We are also inconsistent: [`update(first, last)`](https://json.nlohmann.me/api/basic_json/update/), which is nearly the same operation as object `insert(first, last)`, documents only the **basic** guarantee.

### Comparison: Boost.JSON

Boost.JSON does promise more (`array.hpp` and `object.hpp` on develop, 349862a097c9). `array::insert` is strong for all overloads except an input-iterator range, which is basic. `object::insert(first, last)` is strong for forward iterators. They can afford it because they own the container and relocate elements without throwing. We delegate to `array_t`/`object_t` and have to rebuild the rollback on top, which is what makes this PR verbose.

### Not just the docs

With `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS`, a failed `insert()` leaves stale parent pointers, and the next `assert_invariant()` aborts. That violates even the **basic** guarantee, so it needs a fix whatever we document.

### Proposal

Dropping the strong guarantee where the standard doesn't give it wouldn't break anything, because it never held:

1. Keep **strong** for the single-element overloads. Insert at `end()` directly, since the standard covers that case. Anywhere else, copy first and insert by move, as libstdc++ does internally. `insert(pos, basic_json&&)` already does this.
2. Document **basic** for `insert(pos, cnt, val)`, `insert(pos, first, last)`, `insert(pos, ilist)` and object `insert(first, last)`, worded like `update()`: the value may be partially modified but stays valid.
3. Always restore the parent pointers, also on the exception path (a guard, so `JSON_NOEXCEPTION` builds still compile).
4. Keep the allocation-failure test. For the basic-guarantee overloads, check that the value is valid and its parents are correct instead of checking that `dump()` is unchanged.

This drops the append-and-rotate step, the per-member log and rollback for objects, and the new requirement that a custom `object_t` have a strong single-element `insert()`. It should also avoid most of the measured costs, such as +3.5 % on the count insert at the end and +4–5 % for object inserts of existing keys. I haven't measured that.

---
*Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.*

Good point, the four statements only differed in array/object. Fixed in 6adc89c58d: the section now has one statement for overload (1) (strong guarantee) and one for overloads (2) to (5) (basic guarantee), with the object case in parentheses. They are written as plain paragraphs, because `check_structure.py` expects every overload number as a list item as soon as the section has numbered items.
